paras: The P Street shooting claim was an account given in July 1881 by an unnamed Black man held at Police Headquarters in Washington, D.C., who said a crowd had tried to shoot him on P street for cheering for the President. No attack was confirmed, and the papers presented him as one of several "cranks" who had appeared at police headquarters.
The President was then recovering from a wound, and Washington police were receiving a series of callers the press called "cranks".

According to the Evening Critic, the man was "well-dressed and a negro" and was held in a cell at headquarters; the paper did not say why he had been detained. He told a Critic reporter that a white man named Webb intended to assassinate him for expressing admiration of the President and hopes for his recovery. He also said a crowd had tried to shoot him on P street the night before, about July 10, for cheering for the President, and he named some officers at headquarters as members of it.
From his cell he said he did not want the man "hung or imprisoned" and asked only to be able to speak about the President "without being in danger of my life."
No report of an arrest of Webb, an investigation of the P street claim, or the man's release appears in the coverage.

The Evening Critic ran the story locally on July 11 under the headline "They Keep A-Coming, the Cranks," calling the man a "specimen" and writing that he "pretended" to identify officers among his attackers. A shortened Washington dispatch appeared the next day in the Omaha Daily Bee as "A still more peculiar specimen" in a column headed "More 'Cranks' in Washington." The Bee's version kept the Webb threat and the quotation from the cell but dropped the P street crowd and the officers entirely.

Both papers treated his fear as a curiosity: "the tables have been turned," they wrote, since this crank was a target rather than a would-be assassin, and neither reported anyone else's version of the night on P street.

reader.title: P Street shooting claim, Washington, 1881
bases: The only account of violence is the man's own claim that a crowd tried to shoot him on P street; no attack, injury or arrest is otherwise reported, and the papers treated him as a 'crank' (A1, A2).

No one was killed; the man said a crowd tried to shoot him for cheering the President, a political rather than a justice or racial pretext, and the claim is reported only as his own and doubted by the paper (A1).
The Omaha Bee item is a wire version of the same Washington police-headquarters story, not an independent report, and it omits the P street shooting claim, which appears only in the Critic (A1, A2).

accounts.label: The man's own account
accounts.gist: He said a white man named Webb meant to kill him and a crowd tried to shoot him on P street for cheering the President; he wanted no punishment, only to speak freely.

accounts.label: Critic reporter
accounts.gist: The Critic called him a crank who 'fears those who approach him' and said he 'pretended' to identify officers as members of the crowd.

framing.detail: The Critic headed the item 'They Keep A-Coming, the Cranks', called him a 'specimen' and 'the poor negro', and cast doubt on his identification of officers.
The Omaha Bee ran the item as 'A still more peculiar specimen' in a 'More "Cranks" in Washington' wire column within its coverage of the President's condition.

versions.value: A crowd tried to shoot him on P street the previous night.
No attack mentioned; only a fear that Webb intends to assassinate him.

conflicts.note: The wire version is a shortened form of the same story, so the omission is not a denial.

versions.value: He identified officers around headquarters as among the crowd, which the Critic said he 'pretended' to do.

conflicts.note: The only version of the officer claim comes with the paper's own doubt attached.

record_check.dossier: An unverified claim of an attempted shooting by a crowd, reported as a 'crank' story; at most a claimed mob assault.
No attempt is reported except in the man's own account, which the paper doubted.
A white man named Webb and an unsized crowd, per the man's own claim.
Claimed attempted shooting; no shots or wounds reported.
He said he was targeted for expressing admiration of the President and cheering for him.
2 papers (Critic, July 11; Omaha Bee wire, July 12).

info: The alleged P street shooting attempt was 'last night' relative to the Critic of July 11, i.e. about July 10, 1881.
P street, Washington, D.C.; the man was afterwards held in a cell at Police Headquarters.
None against the man; he said he was threatened for expressing admiration of the President and hopes for his recovery, and for cheering the President.
He named a white man called Webb as intending to assassinate him, and said a crowd tried to shoot him; he 'pretended to identify' officers at headquarters as among that crowd.

sources.note: Local item 'They Keep A-Coming, the Cranks': well-dressed Black man in a cell at Police Headquarters fears a white man named Webb; says a crowd tried to shoot him on P street for cheering the President.
quotes: the poor negro fears that a certain white man named Webb, intends to assassinate him for expressing his admiration of the President and his hopes for his recovery.
has pretended to identify some of the officers around Police Headquarters, as among a crowd that tried to shoot him on P street last night, for cheering for the President.
I don't want the man to be hung or imprisoned, but I merely want to be allowed to say what I please in regard to the President without being in danger of my life.
